feedback.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/44d0f3d13ca03a0644b2f28df9200cd521b7b44d625f346e981d2a54165284f5.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=0
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/6a4c15275ba80d01a90b2e010ed95e95f9a75cfa13f8e51db3433f6356949057.png)

For this particular system, we have

$$
{\lambda }_{2}<{\lambda }_{1}<0
$$

thus, ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ is the eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior (dominant eigenvalue).

Since the dominant eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector ${v}_{1}$ as they move towards the origin.

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/f838a055e525a264bf36b8e0478d186fe17753bba8c0088fea01ac7c5c1f8d7a.png)
